title: SLO Attribute Matrix and Capacity Mapping Manual
author: Priya Menon
body:
Overview

Purpose:
This manual defines a practical, attribute-driven approach to authoring SLOs and directly mapping those SLOs to capacity decisions, oncall workflows, and error-budget remediation actions. It is intended for SREs, platform owners, and service SDMs who must translate service-level targets into concrete capacity and operational policy.

Scope:
- Applies to all public inference endpoints, batch embedding pipelines, and internal control-plane services.
- Excludes customer-managed Private deployment bundles (see eng-private-deployments for private-specific capacity guidance).

Goals:
1. Make SLOs actionable: each SLO must include an attribute set that determines capacity policy, alert thresholds, and remediation stage.
2. Reduce ambiguity during burn: error-budget consumption should trigger deterministic capacity and routing actions.
3. Clarify ownership: map each SLO attribute to an owning role and escalation path.

Definitions
- SLI: observable metric (e.g., successful_response_rate, p95_latency_ms, embedding_throughput_per_gpu).
- SLO: target over a rolling window (e.g., successful_response_rate >= 99.95% over 30d).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO.
- Attribute: metadata attached to an SLO which determines operational decisions (see matrix).

SLO Attribute Matrix (canonical fields)
Format: Each SLO must be published with the following attributes; these drive automation and oncall decisions. Use this matrix as a checklist when creating or updating SLOs.

| Attribute | Permissible values / examples | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| slo_id | service-name/metric/window (string) | unique identifier used in dashboards and alerts |
| criticality | business|production|noncritical | determines priority and minimum capacity hedging |
| impact_type | latency|availability|throughput|correctness | guides remediation actions (scale vs. rollbacks vs. quality alerts) |
| window | 7d|30d|90d | defines aggregation for error-budget accounting |
| target | 99.9%|99.95%|99.99%|p95<=120ms | numeric SLO target |
| owner_role | service_owner|platform_sre|api_team | who owns triage and postmortem |
| escalation_level | L1|L2|L3 | who to contact per burn stage |
| capacity_policy | overprovision|hedge|elastic|best-effort | maps to autoscale and reserved capacity decisions |
| cost_sensitivity | low|medium|high | used in trade-off automation (prefer cheaper model variants) |
| fallback_strategy | model-variant|region-failover|degrade-features|reject-low-priority | automated fallback pattern |
| telemetry_signals | list of metric names | signals used to compute SLI and detect regressions |
| burn_action_policy | none|notify|throttle|autoscale|route-away | action triggered at specified burn thresholds |
| burn_thresholds | low:5%|medium:25%|high:50%|exhaust:100% | standard thresholds (percent of error budget) |
| review_cadence | weekly|monthly|quarterly | how often SLO is reviewed |

Note: store the attribute set in the SLO registry (consolidated YAML in config repo) and surface via the SLO metadata API.

Capacity Mapping Rules (operationalized)
The following mapping rules convert SLO attributes into capacity and routing actions. These are deterministic; any deviation requires an ADR.

1) Criticality -> Minimum Reserved Capacity
- business: reserve >= 40% of steady-state peak across two AZs; maintain warm burst pool sized for 30% additional headroom.
- production: reserve >= 25% of steady-state peak across one region; autoscale to 2x baseline for traffic surges.
- noncritical: no reserved commitment; rely on autoscale and FIFO queueing.

2) Impact_type -> Primary Remediation Pattern
- latency/throughput: prefer autoscale and batching configuration changes; adjust GPU batch_size and request concurrency.
- availability: multi-region failover and increased replica counts; enable circuit-breaker fallbacks.
- correctness: roll forward/rollback model, increase deterministic retries, enable synchronous retries with dead-letter monitoring.

3) Cost_sensitivity + capacity_policy -> Scale decisions
- high cost_sensitivity & elastic policy: prefer model-quantized variants, smaller GPU classes, and cross-tenant fairshare throttling before adding reservations.
- low cost_sensitivity & overprovision: add reserved capacity slots and prioritize headroom.

Error-Budget Burn Actions (automated thresholds)
Embed the following three-stage action set in the SLO automation pipeline. Each service's burn_action_policy should point to one of these templates, optionally customized.

Template A (conservative for business-critical SLOs):
- low (>=5% burn in window): create automated Slack summary to owners, annotate SLO dashboard, and schedule short ad-hoc capacity review.
- medium (>=25%): trigger paging to L1, increment autoscale target by +20% for 30 minutes, enable temporary higher-priority routing.
- high (>=50%): page L2, enable regional failover, shift noncritical traffic off the impacted pool, and create incident channel.
- exhaust (>=100%): page L3, escalate to platform oncall and product leads, immediate manual capacity commit or emergency rollback to last known-good model.

Template B (cost-sensitive services):
- low: notify via ticket only.
- medium: throttle non-essential tenants (best-effort lane), enable lower-cost model variant.
- high: degrade non-core features (e.g., streaming -> non-streaming), enforce per-tenant rate limits and burst cooldown.

Ownership and Escalation
- Owner role must be listed on the SLO page and in oncall rotation.
- Escalation policy must include primary paging phone/SMS and secondary Slack pager.
- For cross-team SLOs (shared infra + service), the owning team retains primary responsibility for incident coord; platform SRE provides capacity actions and implementation help.

Operational Runbooks (concise playbooks to act when burn thresholds are hit)
1) On low burn (automated notification) — Owner actions (5–30 min):
   a) Acknowledge the notification, confirm SLI signal sanity (check tags, duplicates, sparse metrics).
   b) Review recent deployments (git commits, model rollouts) in the last 24 hours.
   c) If deployment suspicious, flip to canary/rollback per deployment runbook.
   d) If capacity bound, open capacity review with platform SRE to evaluate autoscale adjustments.

2) On medium burn (paging to L1) — Immediate actions (under 1 hour):
   a) Triage oncall channel and run the standard triage checklist: errors vs latency vs throttling.
   b) Execute safe autoscale: run CLI to temporarily bump target replicas or increase GPU pool (example below).
   c) Activate fallback_strategy if latency spikes persist after autoscale.
   d) Start an incident document and set severity per incident-rating guidelines.

3) On high/exhaust (L2/L3 escalation) — Rapid mitigation (under 2 hours):
   a) Open incident bridge, invite product and platform leads.
   b) If autoscale insufficient, trigger region failover and re-route traffic via the smart-router (policy: prefer lower-latency region with capacity).
   c) Throttle low-priority tenants and shift costly workloads to queued processing.
   d) Prepare rollback or hotfix; if model-quality issue, roll model to previous version.

Telemetry and Alerting (concrete thresholds and example queries)
- Primary SLI metrics (examples):
  - successful_response_rate (count_success / count_total) over 30d window; alert when rolling SLI drops below target minus 0.01 * target at either low/medium threshold depending on policy.
  - p95_latency_ms service-level: alert if p95 > configured threshold for > 5m.
  - embedding_throughput_per_gpu: used for capacity planning; alert if sustained < 70% expected throughput for 30m (possible degradation or misconfiguration).

Grafana/PromQL examples (text):
- Successful response rate (30d rolling):
  sum_over_time(rate(http_requests_total{job="svc-api",code!~"5.."}[5m])[30d:5m]) / sum_over_time(rate(http_requests_total{job="svc-api"}[5m])[30d:5m])

- p95 latency (5m):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket{job="svc-api"}[5m])) by (le))

CLI examples (platform SRE procedures):
- Increase GPU pool by 20% (example):
  redwoodctl capacity adjust --pool inference-prod-eu --scale +20 --duration 30m --reason "SLO medium burn"

- Temporarily route low-priority traffic away from pool:
  redwoodctl routing update --name smart-router --action blackhole --filter tenant_priority<=low --duration 60m --reason "SLO high burn"

Capacity Simulation and Run Rate Estimation
- Use the capacity-sim tool to compute headroom given recent traffic and model token rates:
  capacity-sim --traffic-csv last_7d.csv --model-profile llama-2-70b-q8 --target-utilization 0.6 --output projection.csv
- Recommended target_utilization values by criticality: business 0.55, production 0.65, noncritical 0.75. Lower target_utilization increases resilience at cost of additional reserved spend.

Quarterly SLO Review Checklist (owners must complete)
- Verify SLO attributes are still correct (criticality, cost_sensitivity, fallback_strategy).
- Re-run capacity-sim with last 90d traffic; confirm reserved capacity meets policy.
- Audit any error-budget burn events and close associated action items in the postmortem.
- Confirm dashboard traces and alerts are still valid and not noisily firing.

Governance and ADRs
- Any deviation from the Attribute Matrix mapping rules (e.g., choosing not to enable autoscale for a production SLO) must be captured in an ADR and approved by platform SRE and service owner.

Appendix A — Example SLO specification (YAML snippet to store in registry)

slo_id: svc-embed/successful_response_rate/30d
criticality: production
impact_type: availability
window: 30d
target: "99.95%"
owners: ["svc-embed-team"]
escalation_level: L2
capacity_policy: hedge
cost_sensitivity: medium
fallback_strategy: model-variant
telemetry_signals: ["http_requests_total","http_request_errors","p95_request_latency_ms"]
burn_action_policy: templateA
burn_thresholds: "low:5%|medium:25%|high:50%|exhaust:100%"
review_cadence: monthly

Appendix B — Decision matrix examples (text):
- If p95 latency spikes but throughput and error rate are normal, prioritize batching tuning and kernel selection before adding GPUs.
- If error rate increases with new model rollout, prefer rollback + postmortem over immediate capacity spend.

Notes and references
- This manual complements the broader capacity governance and error budget handbook; use this document for operationalizing SLO metadata into concrete actions.
- For private deployment variations, consult eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops.
